### Acknowledgments

Some of the information here comes from Software Carpentry's course titled, [Version Control with Git](https://swcarpentry.github.io/git-novice).

## Why Git?

::: {.contnet-visible when-profile="book"}
We’ll start by exploring how version control can be used to keep track of what one person did and when. Even if you aren’t collaborating with other people, automated version control is much better than this situation:
:::

!["notFinal.doc" by Jorge Cham, https://www.phdcomics.com](https://swcarpentry.github.io/git-novice/fig/phd101212s.png)

## What is Git?

-   Distributed version control: Every collaborator has a full copy of the project history on their local machine.

-   Time travel: Revert to any previous state of your code

### Commits

-   A commit is a snapshot of your entire project at a specific point in time.

-   Every commit is identified by a unique 40-character SHA-1 ID.

-   Commit message documents *what* was changed and *why*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
### Commits
:::

![Image courtesy of Software Carpentry](https://swcarpentry.github.io/git-novice/fig/play-changes.svg)

### Branches & Merging

-   Isolated environments: Branching allows you to diverge from the main line of development and work without affecting the stable codebase.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
### Branches & Merging
:::

![Image courtesy of Software Carpentry](https://swcarpentry.github.io/git-novice/fig/versions.svg)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
### Branches & Merging
:::

-   Merging: The process of bringing independent lines of development back together, combining new features with the main branch.

-   Conflict resolution: Git manages overlapping changes, prompting for manual intervention only when files are edited in the exact same place.

![Image courtesy of Software Carpentry](https://swcarpentry.github.io/git-novice/fig/merge.svg)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
### Branches & Merging
:::

### Distributed version control

As mentioned above, every collaborator has a full copy of the project history. Let's pick up where we left off with the scenario above. Now that we have developed a workflow, we want to use it on a compute cluster.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
### Distributed version control
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="book"}
We now have two copies of our codebase, which we will manage with GitHub. Notice that we only pulled the main branch to the cluster, since we've decided that don't really need the development branch there.
:::

![Code is pushed from our laptop to GitHub and then pulled down to the compute cluster.](/general_course_materials/assets/intro_git_tree/intro_git_tree_Page_06.png)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
### Distributed version control
:::

We've started working on a new feature on our laptop, and after running a couple of analyses, we discover and fix a bug on the cluster.

![Our code is quickly diverging, but git will keep us organized.](/general_course_materials/assets/intro_git_tree/intro_git_tree_Page_07.png)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
### Distributed version control
:::

We want to include the bug fix in our development branch, so let's move those changes over to our laptop and merge `c7` into dev.

![Bug fix is, pushed to GitHub, pulled to our laptop and merged into dev.](/general_course_materials/assets/intro_git_tree/intro_git_tree_Page_08.png)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
### Distributed version control
:::

Once we finish the new feature, we can merge it into out main branch and push/pull it onto the server.

![Push updated repository to GitHub and pull changes to the cluster.](/general_course_materials/assets/intro_git_tree/intro_git_tree_Page_09.png)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}

## Branching Strategies

* Why use branches? To enable parallel development by isolating the main codebase from
  * New features
  * Bug fixes
  * Experiments

A number branching strategies have been proposed, each with different use cases [@haddad_what_2022].


### GitFlow

GitFlow is a heavy, structured branching strategy proposed by @driessen_successful_2010 that has received a lot of attention over the years.

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## GitFlow
:::

* Main branches:
  * `master` or `main`: Stable, production-ready code
  * `dev` or `develop`: Latest integrated code for the next release

* Supporting branches:
  * `feature/*`: New features development
  * `release/*`: New production release preparation
  * `hotfix/*`: Quick patches to production issues

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## GitFlow
:::

* Pros:
  * Allows for parallel development on a large scale
  * Excellent for managing multiple versions of a product.

* Cons:
  * Can be overly complex and cumbersome for simple projects.
  * Slows down the CI/CD process.

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## GitFlow
:::

![GitFlow diagram](https://nvie.com/img/git-model@2x.png)


### GitHub Flow

GitHub Flow is a simpler, continuous-delivery-focused strategy [@noauthor_github_nodate], where the `main` branch is always in a deployable state.

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## GitHub Flow
:::

* Workflow:
  1.  Create a descriptive `feature` branch from `main`.
  2.  Commit changes to the `feature` branch.
  3.  Open a Pull Request (PR) to discuss and review changes.
  4.  Merge the `feature` branch into `main`.
  5.  Deploy to production.

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## GitHub Flow
:::

* Pros:
  * Simple, easy to understand, and fast.
  * Ideal for teams with continuous integration and deployment.

* Cons:
  * Not suitable for managing multiple versions or environments.
  * Requires a high level of testing and discipline to keep `main` stable.

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## GitHub Flow
:::

![GitHub Flow diagram](https://www.abtasty.com/wp-content/uploads/github-flow-branching-model.jpeg)

### GitLab Flow

GitLab Flow is a hybrid strategy that combines elements of GitFlow and GitHub Flow [@noauthor_what_nodate].

* Key Feature: Uses environment branches (e.g., `production`, `staging`) in addition to the `main` branch.

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## GitLab Flow
:::

* Workflow:
  1.  Start a `feature` branch from `main`.
  2.  Open a Merge Request (MR) to merge into `main`.
  3.  `main` branch is automatically deployed to a testing environment.
  4.  Merge `main` into a `staging` branch, which is deployed to the staging environment.
  5.  Merge `staging` into a `production` branch, which is deployed to the production environment.

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## GitLab Flow
:::

* Pros:
  * Provides more structure and isolation than GitHub Flow.
  * Works well for projects with multiple deployment environments.

* Cons:
  * Doesn't include extra branches for management of multiple versions
  * Parallel development for large projects may be challenging

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## GitLab Flow
:::

![GitLab Flow diagram](https://res.cloudinary.com/dpdm96hjl/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1670587534/khuibeom.com/docs/gitflow.png)

### Trunk-Based Development

Trunk-based development is a strategy where developers merge small, frequent changes directly into a single, shared "trunk" or `main` branch.

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## Trunk-Based Development
:::

* Core principle: All developers work on the same branch.

* Key practices:
  * Commit small, isolated changes multiple times a day.
  * Use feature flags to hide incomplete work from users.
  * The `main` branch is always in a releasable state.

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## Trunk-Based Development
:::

* Pros:
  * Enables rapid and continuous integration and delivery.
  * Minimizes merge conflicts and "merge hell."

* Cons:
  * Requires a mature, *disciplined* team and strong automated testing.
  * Can be challenging for new developers.


## Choosing a Strategy

* Simplicity vs. Complexity: Choose a strategy that matches your team's size and project's needs.

* Release cycle: A strategy should align with your release cadence (e.g. frequent, continuous, or scheduled).

* Team discipline: The simpler the strategy, the more discipline is required from the team.


## GitHub

-   Remote Hosting: The centralized home for your git repositories in the cloud

-   Collaboration Tools: Integrated issue tracking, project boards, and wikis

-   Code Security: Automated vulnerability scanning and secret detection for your repositories

### Collaborative Review via Pull Request (PR)

<!-- continue on GitHub for these features, what is a good example to show for this? -->

-   PRs allow you to propose changes and invite team members to review your code

-   100% visibility into code changes before they are finalized

-   Inline comments and reviews ensure that all code meets project standards before merging
